text: The Arabic alphabet contains twenty-eight letters — consonants and long vowels — plus fourteen symbols that act as short vowels, pronunciation markers, or grammatical markers.

text: Formal Arabic has only three::how many vowel qualities — a, i, u — each short or long; spoken Arabic adds e and o.
back: Cue: vowel length distinguishes emphatic consonants from their plain counterparts — listen for it.

text: In this book's transliteration, emphatic sounds are marked by UPPERCASE letters (S vs s), and long vowels by doubled vowels (aa, ii, uu).
back: Ex: S = emphatic ص while s = plain س; aa is held longer than a .

text: The four major characteristics that set Arabic script apart from European ones: it is written right to left; letters connect in both print and script; letters change shape by position (initial / medial / final); the script has two layers — a consonant-and-long-vowel skeleton, plus the vowelling.
back: Cue: four — direction, connection, position, layers.

text: The Arabic writing system is regularly phonetic: a one-to-one correspondence between sound and letter — words are written the way they are pronounced.
back: Distinguish: English spelling is the opposite — think though / tough / through .

text: Arabic is written and read from right to left.
back: Cue: books and magazines open the "other way" from English ones.

text: The Levantine dialect group covers the Syrian, Lebanese, Palestinian, and Jordanian dialects.
back: Cue: the Levant = the eastern Mediterranean coast region.

text: The book's map shows 20::how many countries where Arabic is the main language of education and daily life. Grouped west to east: North Africa, the Nile and the Horn, the Levant, Mesopotamia and the northern Gulf, and southern and eastern Arabia.
back: Cue: five regions, west to east — the anchor for the five roster cards. Roster: Morocco · Mauritania · Algeria · Tunisia · Libya · Egypt · Sudan · Somalia · Jordan · Israel/Palestine · Lebanon · Syria · Iraq · Kuwait · Saudi Arabia · Qatar · Bahrain · United Arab Emirates · Oman · Yemen

text: The vowelling layer (vocalization) is normally omitted in written Arabic — readers recognize words without it.
back: Pitfall: your textbook prints vowels while you learn; newspapers will not.

text: Arabic letters are connected in both print AND script — unlike Latin letters, which connect only in handwriting.
back: Why: this is why letters change shape by position — they must join their neighbors.

text: Polite behavior requires you to say hello to everyone in a room or place you enter — including a loosely defined "space" someone regularly occupies.
back: Ex: an outdoor work area, or a guard's position outside a building. Cue: entering = greeting; the room does not have to have walls.

back: Cue: MSA — Dimashq Ex: ana min madiinat Dimashq — "I am from the city of Damascus." Pitfall: the English name Damascus and the Arabic Dimashq share almost nothing — you cannot guess this one.

text: ‎تاب Transliteration: taab he repented — drill 2 — she offered this one as optional extra
back: Cue: MSA — taab Pitfall: nothing to do with an English "tab". She said so directly: "not the English tab, Arabic taab , he repented." Distinguish: she marked baab as required and this one as extra — "if you want to learn extra, you could add that one."

text: A word that begins with a glottal stop has to be written with a hamza on its alif — above the alif for a and u, below it for i. The one word that takes no hamza at all is the definite article al- .
back: Why: she taught it as a listening test — if you hear a word start with a glottal stop, think hamza straight away. Ex: ab and umm both take the hamza ; al- does not. Pitfall: the alif still sounds the same either way — the hamza is about how it is written, not how it is said.

text: The NAME of a letter ends in a hamza that the letter itself does not have — so baa, taa and thaa are written باء · تاء · ثاء, not با · تا · ثا.
back: Why: she wrote the names beside the letters on the board and stopped to point the hamza out. Pitfall: she also warned not to confuse the mark hamza with the personal name Hamza, which has a Haa . Ex: waaw and yaa follow the same pattern — واو and ياء.

text: The last of Arabic's three long vowels is yaa, the sound of ee in beep .
back: Cue: imitate a honking car horn — beeeeep! — and exaggerate it to feel the length. Cue: your Unit 1 card teaches the same vowel as ie in piece . Ex: the book's own practice words are beep and street . Dr. Khouri says it: [sound:arabic_khouri_u2_yaa.mp3]

text: After frontal consonants, Damma is pronounced oo as in booth .
back: Pitfall: English u in but and gum is a deep fatHa, NOT a Damma. Cue: your Unit 1 card teaches this same vowel as oo in poodle — one sound, two keywords. Cue: the name Damma refers to ROUNDING — keep your mouth rounded and it comes out right. Why: a deep consonant pulls it deeper, closer to oo in wool .

text: ‎برافو Transliteration: braafoo Bravo! — said on finishing the first four letters of the alphabet
back: Cue: MSA — a borrowed exclamation of praise, written in Arabic letters. Ex: "Bravo! You have learned the first four letters of the Arabic alphabet." Distinguish: aHsanta is her spoken "Good job! Well done!"; this one is specifically Bravo! , and it is the book's word, not hers.

text: Besides vowel quality , Arabic also distinguishes vowel length, and this too can change a word's meaning.
back: Ex: DHaalim — a long alif in the first syllable, a short i in the second. Distinguish: quality is which vowel sound you make (a frontal or a deep alif); length is how long you hold it — Arabic keeps track of both. Cue: alif itself is a long vowel — the one you hear held in DHaalim .

text: ‎توبوا Transliteration: tuubuu repent! — said to a GROUP — the -uu on the end is the plural
back: Cue: MSA — tuubuu Why: the -uu ending is what makes a verb plural. To one person it would be tub . Pitfall: she warned that Arabic plurals are "very inconsistent" and that broken plurals are a 102 topic — do not generalise this ending yet.

text: ‎جَلّابيّة Transliteration: jallabiyya a long robe — the Syrian word for the garment a Saudi calls a thawb
back: Cue: MSA — jallabiyya Distinguish: same garment, different country's word — thawb in Saudi Arabia, jallabiyya in Syria.

text: Each Arabic long vowel has one short vowel that matches it: alif ( aa ) — fatHa waaw ( uu ) — Damma yaa ( ii ) — kasra
back: Cue: the long vowel is a whole LETTER you write on the line; its short partner is only a mark added above or below. Distinguish: same vowel, two lengths — the long one is a letter you write, the short one a mark you add last. Hear them: fatHa [sound:arabic_ab3e_fatha.mp3] Damma [sound:arabic_ab3e_damma.mp3] kasra [sound:arabic_ab3e_kasra.mp3]

text: Of Arabic's three long vowels, waaw is the second::first / second / third, and its sound is that of the exclamation of delight — ooooo!
back: Cue: it shares its shape with the short vowel Damma, which is written as a miniature waaw. Cue: your Unit 1 card teaches the same vowel as oo in poodle . Pitfall: do not confuse it with English o or u ; keep the mouth rounded and hold it. Dr. Khouri says it: [sound:arabic_khouri_u2_waaw.mp3]

text: A short vowel is written on the letter that precedes it, never on one that follows.
back: Why: an Arabic syllable always BEGINS with a consonant, so the mark rides on that consonant — the first letter of its syllable. Cue: writing the vowels is the third and final step — skeleton first, then the dots, then the vowels. Pitfall: in ordinary text the short vowels are usually not written at all.

text: In Arabic, word stress is attracted to the syllable with a long::long or short vowel.
back: Ex: DHaalim — the accent falls on the first syllable, the one with the long alif, not on the short i of the second. Distinguish: vowel length is a property of one vowel (long or short); word stress is a property of the whole word (which syllable carries the accent).

text: ‎تابوت Transliteration: taabuut a casket, a coffin — drill 4, the longest word in it
back: Cue: MSA — taabuut Why: taa + alif + baa + waaw + taa . She used it as the hard one because it carries both a long aa and a long uu . Ex: Sydney wrote it at the board and she said "this is longer" as the class worked through it. Ex: the book's own recording, for comparison [sound:arabic_vocab_u2_le6_taabuut.mp3]

text: An Arabic long vowel is held at least twice as long as a short one — and English has no long vowels at all, so Arabic's should feel exaggerated to you.
back: Pitfall: do not worry about holding one "too long" — stretch it out so you can hear the difference. Why: vowel length changes meaning, and a mispronounced length can make the word unintelligible.

text: English spells two distinct sounds th , and Arabic gives each its own letter. thaa is only the three sound, never the that sound.
back: Cue: thaa carries THREE dots — say "three" out loud before you pronounce or read it. Distinguish: the th of that belongs to dhaal, a letter this course has not taught yet — Unit 1 drilled hearing the two apart.

text: fatHa is written as a short, slanted line segment above::above or below? its consonant.
back: Distinguish: Damma sits in the same place, above the letter, but is shaped like a miniature waaw. Cue: the vowel marks go on last — consonant skeleton first, then the dots, then the vowels.

text: The name kasra means "break", and it refers to your mouth being only slightly open as you say it.
back: Cue: the name describes the MOUTH, not the sound — slightly open, not wide open. Pitfall: do not drop the jaw for it; that turns it into a different vowel.

text: The name of the short vowel fatHa means "opening".
back: Why: it names the shape of your mouth as you say it — wide open. Try it and see. Distinguish: Damma is named for ROUNDING the mouth, not for opening it.

text: In social as well as professional situations it is polite to shake hands when meeting or greeting another person of the same gender::same or opposite?.
back: Why: with the opposite gender it varies widely according to religious belief and personal practice.

text: ‎توت Transliteration: tuut berries, mulberries — the word she built to teach waaw as a long uu
back: Cue: MSA — tuut Why: taa + waaw + taa — the waaw in the middle is the long uu . Ex: she added that for Arab children tuut is also the noise a train makes. Ex: book audio [sound:arabic_vocab_u2_le6_tuut.mp3] Pitfall: she called this REQUIRED, twice — "This is required, write it also."

text: What decides how frontal or how deep a short vowel actually sounds is the consonants surrounding it.
back: Ex: fatHa runs from e in bet to u in but ; kasra from ee in keep to i in bit . Cue: each short vowel swings along the same axis its long partner does.

text: Of the consonants Unit 2 teaches, the frontal ones — the ones that pull a neighbouring short vowel toward the front of the mouth — are baa, taa and thaa.
back: Cue: all three share one skeleton and differ only in their dots — and all three are frontal. Pitfall: the book names these as EXAMPLES of frontal consonants, not as the complete set — Arabic also has deep (emphatic) consonants, which pull the same vowel the other way.

text: A man meeting a woman should wait for her to extend her hand first.
back: Why: her offered hand is the signal that she wants to shake yours.

text: ‎بِالعَرَبي Transliteration: bil-carabi in Arabic — the tail of her vocabulary check: "maa baab ___?"
back: Cue: MSA — bil-carabi Why: bi- is the preposition "in" (the same bi- as in ahlan bika ) stuck onto al-carabi . Ex: she asks maa baab bil-carabi? and wants the meaning back. Pitfall: the c is cayn — say "ah", then start to shock yourself, but only a little.

text: ‎أبي Transliteration: abii my father — ab with the ending that means "my"
back: Cue: MSA — abii Why: the possessive "my" is a yaa stuck on the end of the noun — ab + ii . She wrote it on the board the day she taught yaa . Ex: her own answer when the class asked her — ism abii Elias , "Elijah in English." Distinguish: the same -ii turns baab into baabii , my door.

text: ‎أبوكَ / أبوكِ Transliteration: abuuka / abuuki your father — to a man / to a woman
back: Cue: MSA — abuuka / abuuki Distinguish: -ka to a man, -ki to a woman — the same pair of endings as ismuka / ismuki . Ex: she went round the room asking it, switching gender as she went: "I'm switching between men and women because I'm talking to men and women."

arabic: ما اسم أبوكَ؟ / ما اسم أبوكِ؟
translit: maa ism abuuka? / maa ism abuuki?
text: ‎ما اسم أبوكَ؟ / ما اسم أبوكِ؟ Transliteration: maa ism abuuka? / maa ism abuuki? What is your father's name? — to a man / to a woman — she asked the whole room this
back: Cue: MSA — maa ism abuuka? / maa ism abuuki? Why: no verb "is" — the question is just what + the name of your father . Ex: you answer ism abii + the name. Hers: ism abii Elias . Pitfall: maa goes with a noun, so it is maa here and never hal . Ex: the same question to a woman, in her voice [sound:arabic_khouri_maa_ism_abuuki.mp3]

text: ‎بات Transliteration: baat he slept over — somewhere other than home — drill 2, and the long-aa half of her contrast
back: Cue: MSA — baat Distinguish: baat holds the aa ; bat is the same letters said short. She drilled the pair to show what a long vowel is. Pitfall: nothing to do with the English word "but", which is what it sounds like. Ex: the book's own recording, for comparison [sound:arabic_vocab_u2_le3_baat.mp3]

text: ‎بابي Transliteration: baabii my door — drill 11 — baab with the same "my" ending as abii
back: Cue: MSA — baabii Why: baab + -ii . The -ii is a yaa on the end, exactly as in abii . Ex: book audio [sound:arabic_vocab_u2_d11_baabii.mp3] Ex: at the board she asked "what's baabii ?" and answered it herself — "my door."

text: ‎ثوب Transliteration: thawb a garment — the long white robe a Saudi man wears; also a woman's dress
back: Cue: MSA — thawb Distinguish: in Syria the same garment is a jallabiyya ; in Egypt thawb is closer to a jacket. Why: she built it letter by letter on the board — thaa + waaw + baa .

text: ‎ثواب Transliteration: thawaab a reward — she taught it as the opposite of punishment
back: Cue: MSA — thawaab Distinguish: the opposite of caqaab , punishment — that is how she introduced it, by asking the class for the antonym. Why: another word she built on the board from thaa , waaw and alif .

text: ‎حَرف Transliteration: Harf a letter of the alphabet — the word she uses for the thing she teaches every class
back: Cue: MSA — Harf Pitfall: the capital H is Haa , made in the throat with the muscles tightened — not an English h. Ex: she introduced it while starting the waaw lesson — " Harf waaw ." Ex: she says it as a phrase, never alone — the clip is her Harf waaw , "the letter waaw".

text: ‎بِالإنجليزي Transliteration: bil-ingliizi in English — the other half of her check — she flips between the two to catch you
back: Cue: MSA — bil-ingliizi Ex: maa baab bil-ingliizi? — and the answer she wanted was the English word "door". She said "I tricked you" when the class answered in the wrong language. Distinguish: same bi- + al- frame as bil-carabi ; only the language name changes.

text: ‎أيّ Transliteration: ayy which — the word that makes her question pick ONE out of many: "min ___ madiina anta?"
back: Cue: MSA — ayy Distinguish: ayy asks which one out of a set; ayna asks where. They are different words that look alike in transliteration. Ex: it came up because a student wanted to ask about a city rather than a place.

text: ‎مِن أيّ مدينة أنتَ؟ / أنتِ؟ Transliteration: min ayy madiina anta? / anti? From which city are you? — to a man / to a woman — the city version of min ayna anta
back: Cue: MSA — min ayy madiina anta? / anti? Distinguish: min ayna anta? asks where from in general; this asks specifically which CITY. Ex: her own answer — ana min madiinat Dimashq . Pitfall: ayy and ayna cannot both appear; pick one.

text: ‎سوريا Transliteration: Suuriya Syria — the country she is from
back: Cue: MSA — Suuriya Ex: her full answer to you on 3 Sep — ana min Suuriya, askun fii Lynchburg : I am from Syria, I live in Lynchburg.

c2: the short-vowel marks, as a set
text: ‎تَشكيل Transliteration: tashkiil the short-vowel marks, as a set — fatHa, Damma, kasra and sukuun together
back: Cue: MSA — tashkiil Why: her words — " tashkiil means everything, all short vowels." She then said "you need to learn these words." Pitfall: ordinary written Arabic carries NO tashkiil — not newspapers, not subtitles. You will be weaned off it.

text: ‎أُمّ Transliteration: umm mother — her example of an alif carrying hamza with a Damma
back: Cue: MSA — umm Why: the word opens on a glottal stop with a u sound, so the hamza sits ON TOP of the alif and takes a Damma . Distinguish: ab is father, umm is mother.

text: ‎جاءَ Transliteration: jaa'a he came — her example of a hamza standing alone on the line
back: Cue: MSA — jaa'a Why: at the END of a word a hamza can sit by itself on the line — it is only at the START that it must ride an alif .

text: The -uu that turns a verb plural — as in tuubuu — is called waaw al-jamaaca , literally the waaw of the group.
back: Ex: tub is "repent" to one person; tuubuu is "repent" to a group. Pitfall: this is one plural pattern, not the rule. She called Arabic plurals "very inconsistent" and pushed broken plurals to 102.

text: In many regions children are taught to greet an older, respected guest by shaking hands and then kissing, or being kissed on, both cheeks.
back: Why: it welcomes the guest into the home with warmth and respect.

text: A consonant is a sound that blocks or narrows the airflow.
back: Ex: "syllables in Arabic always begin with a consonant ." Distinguish: a vowel is the open, freely flowing sound; a consonant closes or narrows it. Cue: in Arabic the consonants are the skeleton you write first; the vowels are added last.

text: A short vowel is as long as an ordinary English vowel.
back: Ex: "by convention, short vowels are written above or below the consonant." Distinguish: in Arabic a short vowel is a MARK added above or below a consonant; a long vowel is a whole letter standing on the line. Pitfall: they are usually left unwritten altogether, which is why reading unvowelled Arabic is a separate skill.

text: A syllable is one beat of a word.
back: Ex: " syllables in Arabic always begin with a consonant." Meaning: one beat — a vowel plus the consonants packed around it. Cue: a syllable holding a long vowel is almost always the stressed one. Distinguish: a syllable is heard; a letter is written.

text: At its most frontal, fatHa is e as in bet ; when deep, it is u as in but .
back: Why: it swings along the same frontal-to-deep axis its long counterpart alif does, and the consonants around it decide where it lands. Pitfall: alif and fatHa do NOT share keywords — alif's deep pole is the long a of father , fatHa's is the short u of but . Same colour, different length.

text: ‎ـا Letter: alif Position: medial and final
back: Distinguish: alif never joins to the letter after it, so the following letter always starts fresh. Roster (independent · initial · medial · final): ‎ا ا ـا ـا

text: ‎بـ Letter: baa Position: initial
back: Distinguish: baa is a connector: it joins on both sides, and the dot stays below the body. Roster: baa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial , medial, final.

text: ‎ـبـ Letter: baa Position: medial
back: Distinguish: baa is a connector: it joins on both sides, and the dot stays below the body. Roster: baa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial , final.

text: ‎ـب Letter: baa Position: final
back: Distinguish: baa is a connector: it joins on both sides, and the dot stays below the body. Roster: baa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial, final .

text: ‎تـ Letter: taa Position: initial
back: Distinguish: taa has the same shapes as baa in every position, and it is a connector too — two dots on top instead of one below. Mnemonic: associate the sound t with two dots on top . Roster: taa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial , medial, final.

text: ‎ـتـ Letter: taa Position: medial
back: Distinguish: taa has the same shapes as baa in every position, and it is a connector too — two dots on top instead of one below. Mnemonic: associate the sound t with two dots on top . Roster: taa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial , final.

text: ‎ـت Letter: taa Position: final
back: Distinguish: taa has the same shapes as baa in every position, and it is a connector too — two dots on top instead of one below. Mnemonic: associate the sound t with two dots on top . Roster: taa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial, final .

text: ‎ثـ Letter: thaa Position: initial
back: Distinguish: thaa is a connector, written just like baa and taa in every position, except that it carries three dots above. Roster: thaa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial , medial, final.

text: ‎ـثـ Letter: thaa Position: medial
back: Distinguish: thaa is a connector, written just like baa and taa in every position, except that it carries three dots above. Roster: thaa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial , final.

text: ‎ـث Letter: thaa Position: final
back: Distinguish: thaa is a connector, written just like baa and taa in every position, except that it carries three dots above. Roster: thaa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial, final .

text: ‎يـ Letter: yaa Position: initial
back: Distinguish: yaa's independent and final forms differ from its initial and medial ones, which look like baa, taa and thaa — with two dots below. Roster: yaa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial , medial, final. Dr. Khouri says it: [sound:arabic_khouri_u2_yaa.mp3]

text: ‎ـيـ Letter: yaa Position: medial
back: Distinguish: yaa's independent and final forms differ from its initial and medial ones, which look like baa, taa and thaa — with two dots below. Roster: yaa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial , final. Dr. Khouri says it: [sound:arabic_khouri_u2_yaa.mp3]

text: ‎ـي Letter: yaa Position: final
back: Distinguish: yaa's independent and final forms differ from its initial and medial ones, which look like baa, taa and thaa — with two dots below. Roster: yaa's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial, final . Dr. Khouri says it: [sound:arabic_khouri_u2_yaa.mp3]

text: ‎ـو Letter: waaw Position: medial and final::name both
back: Distinguish: waaw never joins to the letter after it, so its shapes barely change. Roster: waaw's four written forms run right to left across the row — independent, initial, medial , final . Dr. Khouri says it: [sound:arabic_khouri_u2_waaw.mp3]

back: Cue: MSA — ismuka / ismuki Why: possessive pronouns are suffixes — -i = my ( ismi ), -ka = your (m), -ki = your (f). The u in the middle is a vowel on the last letter of ism , so the pieces are ism + u + ka . Distinguish: Levantine ismak / ismik — "the suffix that indicates you-masculine is -ka or -ak."
